EnvId.description:
Identifies one materialisation of a unit. A unit re-materialised after reclaim
gets a new environment, not a new unit.

Outside.description:
One repository outside a home that held a copy of the home's commits.

Read once, when the home is trashed, and never read again as evidence: `gc` proves a
copy by asking the repositories on this disk again, not by believing this row. What
this carries is the name of what the verdict rested on, so that a sweep which finds
the copy gone can say which copy that was.

commits.description: How many of the home's commits it covered. Exact.

references.description:
The refs there that reached those commits, as that repository spells them. A
sample of at most ten, in the order Git listed them.

ProjectId.description: Identifies a project: one Git repository Nodal manages units for.

Record.description:
What a safe verdict rested on, as a row keeps it.

A record and never permission, and the difference is the whole reason it is a second type.
A [`Proof`] is what this machine proved a moment ago; this is what it wrote down. The copy
can go after the home is in the trash — somebody deletes a branch in a clone, a remote
drops a merged branch — so `nodal gc` asks [`judge`] again before it removes the directory
and compares its own fresh proof with this. Nothing turns this back into a proof.

It lives here, beside the row, and not in the kernel. A row is the model's, and a model
that had to import the lifecycle to name its own column would be the dependency running
backwards.

It is transparent over the list it holds, so the row and the schema are exactly what they
were before the type existed: the discipline is in the Rust type and none of it reaches
the document.

[`Proof`]: crate::lifecycle::kernel::Proof
[`judge`]: crate::lifecycle::kernel::judge

Rested.description:
What a reclaim's uniqueness check decided about the home it trashed.

Three answers and not two, because "nothing was written down" is a third fact and
reading it as either of the others would be a claim this machine did not make.

oneOf.description:
The row says nothing, which is what a row an older Nodal wrote says. `gc` reads
the home again and believes only what that reading shows it.

The check found nothing that existed only in the home. `copies` names the
repositories and refs that held the commits it did not refuse over, and it is
empty for a home that had no commit of its own to hold.

The row carries a [`Record`] and not a [`crate::lifecycle::kernel::Proof`], and that is
the point of the two types. A proof is what one reading proved, and only
[`crate::lifecycle::kernel::judge`] makes one; this is what was written down, and `gc`
asks the kernel again rather than reading this as permission. Nothing turns it back
into a proof. A `Record` is transparent over the list, so the row and its schema are
exactly what they were before the type existed.

copies.description: What held them, one entry per repository.

oneOf.description:
The check found work that existed only in the home and `--force` went on. The
person looked and said so, so the retention running out removes the directory
as it always did.

Slug.description: The CLI handle for a unit, derived from its branch.

Timestamp.description: A UTC instant, serialised as an RFC 3339 string.

UnitId.description: Identifies a `WorkUnit`. Stable for the life of the work, across machines.

description: One reclaimed home, kept until it expires.

environment_id.description:
The materialisation whose home this was. One row per environment: an
environment is reclaimed once.

expires_at.description: The first instant `nodal gc` may remove it.

home.description: Where the home was while it was live.

project_id.description: The project that unit belongs to, so `gc` can sweep one project's trash.

pruned_bytes.description:
What the prune dropped from the copy on its way in: the build output and the
installed dependencies the home was keeping warm, in bytes.

Zero is the honest answer for a home that held none, for one an ignore rule
covered none of, and for a row written before Nodal pruned anything at all.
Defaulted on the way in for that last case: a journalled reclaim from an older
Nodal has no such field and still has to be rebuilt and finished.

rested.description:
What the uniqueness check decided, and what it rested on.

Defaulted on the way in: a row written before this field says nothing, which is
[`Rested::Unrecorded`] and not a claim that the home was safe.

slug.description: The unit's handle, kept here so a listing reads without a join to a unit row.

snapshot.description:
The ref a `--force` reclaim committed the work to, inside the trashed
repository. `None` when the home was clean and nothing had to be preserved.
